title: Redwood edge cases demo: long context & high TPS
next_steps: Alex Chen - Send tailored pricing for Dedicated + pilot options by 2025-09-19
Priya Patel - Share demo recording and console walkthrough link (edge-cases deck) by EOD
Customer - Provide sample workload (1 day trace / traffic profile) for benchmark by 2025-09-22
action_items: Alex Chen - Pricing + Dedicated capacity options - due 2025-09-19
Priya Patel - Console + Optimize screenshots + batching recommendation export - due 2025-09-16

summary: Short demo focused on edge cases: long context workflows (large conversation history & document retrieval), high TPS loads for embeddings and chat, streaming backpressure and timeouts. Discussed architectural tradeoffs (hosted vs Dedicated), caching/batching levers, and monitoring in Redwood Console & Optimize. Agreed next step: provide workload trace and run a short pilot/benchmark on Dedicated.
topics: Observability in Redwood Console and Optimize
questions: How does Redwood handle partial responses when streaming is interrupted?
What QoS/backpressure signals are available to clients?
What guardrails for timeouts and retries do you recommend?
transcript:
Header: 2025-09-15 16:00 PDT | Duration: 47m | Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood Product), Marta (Acme Head ML), Devon (Platform), Samir (SRE), Lina (PM)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Alex from Redwood, I'll kick off, Priya will drive the demo, Jordan is on for product q's. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Marta: Marta here.
[00:15] Devon: Devon - hi.
[00:18] Samir: Samir on.
[00:20] Lina: Lina here.
[00:22] Alex: Awesome. We're gonna focus today on three edge cases you called out — long context (think 50k-100k tokens), really high TPS for embeddings + chat, and streaming/backpressure behavior that’s been causing client timeouts. Priya do you want to share screen?
[00:32] Priya: Yep, sharing now. Sorry small delay. So first slide is the quick architecture: hosted API, Dedicated pools, and our Private option for VPCs, etc. Note — some of the product names in the slides are abbreviated, sorry, it's our internal deck link: /redwood/edge-cases-deck.pdf
[01:05] Priya: Ok, long-context — customers typically approach this in two ways: one, native long-context models (65k windows), or two, retrieval + context stitching with KV/prefix cache. For Acme you mentioned large contract histories per user, right?
[01:18] Marta: Yeah we're storing years of conversations and contract attachments. We need context to persist across sessions, sometimes 30-60k tokens per request, and some calls spike in volume. Latency and cost are both big concerns.
[01:29] Priya: Totally. So for long context we demoed two patterns: 1) model-native long windows (we onboarded a 65k model in this demo env) and 2) retrieval where Redwood's KV cache keeps hot prefix tokens on GPU memory to avoid re-encoding repeated history. The tradeoff — native long context is simpler but increases per-token compute; KV/prefix cache can make 10-20x effective speedups for repeated prefixes but needs orchestration.
[01:55] Devon: Quick question — how do you keep the KV cache consistent across replicas? We run multi-AZ nodes and often traffic hits different hosts.
[02:05] Priya: Good q. Our runtime has a sharded KV layer with replication; small prefixes are kept on the serving GPU and also backed to a fast k-v store in RAM on the node. We use smart routing so requests that can benefit from local cache go to the host with warm entries. There's slight eventual consistency in corner cases but we provide TTL and consistency metrics in Console.
[02:30] Samir: You said 'smart routing' — is that sticky routing? We worry about uneven load and hotspots.
[02:36] Priya: It's workload-aware. You can enable affinity for sessions, or let the router pick lowest-latency host. For Dedicated customers we offer stronger locality guarantees because the pool is reserved.
[02:45] Marta: On long-context cost — is quantization compatible with 65k models? We've seen accuracy drop with heavy quant.
[02:52] Priya: Short answer: yes, but careful. Redwood Optimize recommends quantization profiles per workload — for very sensitive QA over contracts we might recommend 8-bit fine-tuned profiles or mixed quant. Optimize's evaluation harness can run a small regression test against your prompt set to validate.
[03:12] Priya: Next, high TPS. You said embeddings + chat can hit sustained thousands of reqs per second during peak batch jobs?
[03:19] Lina: Yep, nightly enrichment job creates embeddings for millions of docs; spikes during reindex. Also prod chat has sudden user surges.
[03:26] Alex: For high TPS we demoed Dedicated pools with fixed throughput and autoscaling buffers. Key levers: batching window, max batch size, and autoscaler headroom. Priya show the Console TPS chart please.
[03:38] Priya: Screen — Console > Model routes > Throughput. You'll see simulated load: we push 3k rps for embeddings with microbatching enabled. You can see latency distribution and token cost per minute. Also Optimize suggests batching config to reduce tokens/second CPU wall.
[03:56] Devon: Are there recommended batch sizes for embeddings vs streaming chat? We tried big batches and saw tail latency spikes.
[04:04] Priya: Embeddings tolerate larger batches since it's synchronous; chat streaming needs smaller batches and prioritization. Our runtime supports continuous batching: it will emit partial tokens to streaming clients while still gathering small groups for efficiency; that reduces tail latency. But you need careful timeout configs on the client side.
[04:24] Samir: That leads into our streaming/backpressure problem — when clients disconnect during long streams we see lots of half-open connections and a memory leak. How does Redwood surface that?
[04:35] Priya: We have multiple signals: connection state metrics, server-side streaming errors, and backpressure counters. We expose these in Console and you can set alerts. Also on the protocol layer we support gRPC streaming and chunked HTTP; the server gives a soft backpressure signal when the request queue is full (503 with Retry-After or explicit flow-control headers).
[04:58] Marta: Do you recommend client-side quotas or server-side sheds? We want graceful degradation — not full 503s.
[05:05] Priya: Best practice is layered: client should set per-request timeouts and retry with exponential backoff; server-side you can use circuit-breakers and fallback to smaller model variants or cached responses. Redwood supports automatic model-fallback policies (e.g., if 65k variant is overloaded, fall back to 16k window variant with a brief note). The Console shows drop rates and fallback counts.
[05:28] Lina: A concrete example: we had endpoints timing out after 30s and clients retried immediately, amplifying the spike. What's the recommended timeout and retry policy?
[05:37] Alex: We typically recommend request timeout << user-visible timeout. For interactive chat, client visible 10s, set request timeout 8s, and retries with jitter only for idempotent calls. For streaming, use short initial window and accept partial responses. Also enable request hedging for critical reads.
[05:54] Devon: Hedging increases load though — does Redwood account for double requests in billing?
[06:00] Priya: Hedging is configurable; we expose effective cost numbers in Optimize so you can model the tradeoff. For critical low-latency reads we see customers accept 10-20% extra cost for 40-60% tail AWS improvement.
[06:16] Alex: I'll pause and show the demo flow: 1) Console walkthrough of a high-TPS embeddings route; 2) live run of a long-context 65k prompt; 3) streaming demo showing backpressure handling. Priya, go to the embeddings run.
[06:30] Priya: (screen) Here's embeddings route, route config has batching window 25ms, max batch 256, autoscaler target 1200 rps. You can toggle 'aggressive batching' and see predicted token cost. We'll start the synthetic load.
[06:50] [Synthetic load run — simulated 3k rps for 90s, graph shows p50/p95/p99 latency lines]
[07:30] Priya: You can see p99 spikes when the autoscaler is cold; Dedicated solves that with pre-warmed instances, or you can increase burst capacity. Also shown is the Optimize suggestion: reduce batching window to 15ms but increase CPU for latency-sensitive chat.
[07:50] Marta: The graph shows a steady token cost increase during spikes — can you send the exact CSV export?
[07:55] Priya: Yep I'll export and attach after the call (see action items).
[08:02] Priya: Next the long-context live run. I'll load a 58k token prompt (slightly noisy transcription of some names in the sample but it's realistic) — note this was anonymized sample.
[08:18] [Live run start — Streaming response begins]
[08:25] Priya: You'll see that we stream partial tokens as the model generates while KV cache is warming; for repeated prefixes the latency drops dramatically on subsequent calls.
[08:40] Samir: When you stream partial tokens, if the client disconnects mid-stream, does the model computation continue server-side or is it aborted? Our memory leak came from aborted compute still holding kv-resources.
[08:52] Priya: Good catch. We cancel compute on client disconnect by default — we free GPU KV state after a short grace period (configurable). For long-running pipelines you can change the grace to allow downstream to reconnect. Also we show graceful cancellation metrics in the Console so you can tune.
[09:09] Lina: You mentioned a 'grace period' — what is default?
[09:12] Priya: Default is 10s; can be 0 for immediate abort or up to minutes if you opt in. But watch cost.
[09:21] Devon: We use ALB timeouts that close idle TCP at 60s which sometimes cut streams; is there a keepalive or heartbeat recommended?
[09:29] Priya: Yes, use HTTP chunked keepalive pings or gRPC keepalive. We surface best-practice examples in our SDK.
[09:36] Alex: Now to a failure mode demo — backpressure. We'll throttle the backend to induce queue saturation and show how Redwood responds. Priya?
[09:45] [Throttle simulation — queue builds up, server emits 503 + Retry-After header, fallback to smaller model triggered]
[10:02] Priya: You can see the router returning explicit flow-control headers and the Console alarm firing. Also Optimize highlights the recommend batch config to reduce this.
[10:12] Marta: Are Retry-After headers configurable? We want short retry windows for interactive stuff.
[10:17] Priya: Yep configurable per-route. You can also add custom traffic shaping rules to prioritize VIP routes.
[10:24] Samir: About timeouts: if the client waits 30s then retries and we have a fallback to smaller model which returns faster but lower quality — how do we surface that to the application? We need meta indicating fallback reason.
[10:37] Priya: We attach a response header X-Redwood-Model-Warn with variant and reason (e.g., 'fallback:capacity'). Also the console logs include request_id mapping to the model used. We can optionally include a small structured JSON in the response explaining fallback.
[10:52] Marta: Ok good. On security briefly — we need to be able to use our KMS and must have audit logs for every tokenized request. Do you support customer-managed keys and SAML SSO?
[11:05] Alex: Yes: KMS integrations (customer-managed), SOC 2 compliant infra, SAML/SSO + RBAC. Audit logs are exportable to your SIEM; for Private there's full control plane in your VPC. We'll share the security pack.
[11:19] Marta: Great. Also need to confirm data retention and deletion policies for embeddings, since those are derived artifacts.
[11:26] Jordan (product): By default hosted API does not retain user content beyond operational logs; Dedicated can be set with no retention and opt-out of logging. We'll include the exact text in the security doc.
[11:40] Priya: Back to performance — a few practical knobs that managers typically use: 1) autoscaler target and burst capacity, 2) max batch and batching window, 3) model-fallback policies, 4) pre-warm Dedicated nodes for predictable p99. Optimize will generate profiles recommending exact numbers based on your trace.
[12:05] Marta: Can Optimize take our sample trace and output a recommended config?
[12:09] Priya: Yes — upload the trace to Optimize and it will simulate different configs and provide cost/latency tradeoffs. We'll run an initial job as part of the pilot.
[12:18] Devon: For the embeddings large batch job we want to use spot GPUs to save cost — does Redwood support spot for Dedicated?
[12:26] Alex: Yes, we support mixed pools: on-demand + spot. For steady-state low-latency we recommend on-demand; for batch offline jobs, spot + autoscale works well. Billing and preemption metrics are shown in Console.
[12:40] Samir: On metrics, does Console expose per-token cost by route and by time window? We need hourly granularity for billing back to teams.
[12:48] Priya: Yep per-route per-token cost with exportable CSVs and cost attribution tags. You can tag requests by customer_id or workspace.
[12:58] Marta: Ok real quick — do you have any limitations on request body size or multipart attachments for long docs?
[13:05] Priya: We accept up to X MB per request in the hosted API by default; for very large docs we recommend chunking or using our upload artifact store and referencing it in the prompt. Private deployments can customize limits. I'll follow up with exact numbers in the doc.
[13:20] Lina: You mentioned upload artifact store — is that part of Redwood or a partner?
[13:24] Priya: It's Redwood-managed object store with optional customer-managed S3 backend for Private.
[13:31] Alex: We're about halfway through; any other burning topics?
[13:35] Samir: One more: how do you detect model regression when we change quantization? We can't afford subtle hallucinations on contracts.
[13:44] Priya: Optimize's eval harness runs regression tests against a saved prompt set and flags differences with diffing metrics. You can tie that into alerting so changes in quality beyond a threshold block rollouts.
[13:58] Marta: Good — show us the eval UI.
[14:02] Priya: (screen) Here's Optimize > Evals, you upload baseline prompts and expected outputs (or automated scoring rules). It runs across model variants and quant profiles and gives per-sample diffs. We put a gate on rollout.
[14:20] [Short demo of eval run — shows a couple of flagged samples where heavy 4-bit quant introduced minor token-level diffs]
[14:40] Priya: Finally we demo a long-running pilot blueprint: 1) provide a 24h trace, 2) Redwood runs an Optimize simulation, 3) run a small Dedicated pilot with pre-warm, 4) evaluate regressions and then scale. Typical pilot 2-4 weeks.
[14:58] Marta: That timeline works. What's the pricing model for pilot? Discounted reserved capacity?
[15:06] Alex: We usually offer a short-term reserved burst with usage credits; I'll include options in the pricing doc.
[15:14] Lina: Can we see sample SLA numbers for Dedicated? p99 latency SLOs?
[15:20] Alex: We'll send the SLA matrix. For Dedicated we offer SLO-backed throughput and uptime with escalation. Details in the enterprise pack.
[15:28] Devon: A few nitty gritty infra questions — do you run on k8s, what underlying scheduler?
[15:34] Jordan: Our serving runtime runs on a custom scheduler layered on top of k8s for orchestration. The runtime is optimized for GPU kernels, and we pick kernels based on sequence and batch characteristics. Sometimes transcriptions in older docs call it 'kube-shedule' — ignore that typo.
[15:50] Samir: Any limits on concurrent streams per GPU?
[15:55] Priya: It's config-driven, typical Dedicated config allows dozens of concurrent small streams per GPU depending on model. We can share benchmarking numbers for your exact model.
[16:05] Marta: Ok let's talk about the specific Acme workload — we have two main paths: 1) nightly embedding enrichment (high throughput, batch-friendly), 2) interactive contract QA (long context, sensitive accuracy). For the enrichment job we can probably use spot Dedicated. For contract QA we prefer reserved on-demand with strict evals. Does Redwood support mixed routing?
[16:26] Alex: Yes you can have multiple routes: enrichment route uses a spot pool with high batching; QA route uses reserved Dedicated with stricter SLOs and different model variants. We'll set RBAC so only certain teams can hit QA route.
[16:40] Marta: We want to instrument fallbacks — if QA route is down fall back to 'readonly cached answers' rather than a lower-quality model. Is that supported?
[16:49] Priya: You can define a fallback chain: cached answer -> model-fallback -> degrade to degrade-mode response. The router supports prioritized fallbacks.
[16:58] Devon: One of our worries is billing surprises with retries/fallbacks. Can Optimize forecast the cost including hedging and fallbacks?
[17:06] Priya: Yes it simulates worst-case and typical-case cost and gives confidence intervals.
[17:15] [We jump ahead to some audience Q&A — some crosstalk and interruptions]
[18:02] Marta: In the console demo you flagged a p99 of 2.1s — what model was that?
[18:07] Priya: That was the 16k window variant with mixed-quant profile. The 65k variant had a higher p99 ~4.8s in that synthetic run.
[18:20] Samir: Can we throttle by customer_id tag at the router to protect critical customers?
[18:25] Priya: Absolutely — request tagging and per-tag rate limits exist. You can do per-customer throttles, per-route, per-org.
[18:33] Lina: For the embeddings pipeline we want to stream partial results to downstream consumers — any caveats?
[18:40] Priya: Make sure to use idempotent chunking and checkpoint tokens so replays don't duplicate. We provide examples in SDK.
[18:48] Devon: A practical ask — can Redwood include an initial lighthouse benchmark against our sample trace as part of pilot?
[18:55] Alex: Yes — that's one of the standard deliverables. We'll run a 48-hour perf and cost benchmark and deliver results.
[19:02] Marta: Great. Any more product constraints we missed?
[19:07] Samir: How do you handle tokenization differences across model variants in caching?
[19:13] Priya: We normalize tokenization at the router and store canonical token IDs in KV. When falling back to a smaller model with different tokenizer, we have translation layers that attempt to map tokens, but there are edge cases. We show token-diff metrics in Optimize.
[19:30] Alex: Wrapping toward close — quick recap: we'll get your trace, run Optimize sims, run a Dedicated pilot with pre-warm and fallback policy, share pricing + SLA + security pack. Anything to add?
[19:44] Marta: Please include an explicit rollback / abort plan for the pilot — we need fast rollback if regression detected.
[19:49] Alex: Noted. Priya — any final notes?
[19:52] Priya: We'll attach console exports and Optimize recommendations. Expect deliverables by 2025-09-19 for pricing and by 2025-09-22 for the initial benchmark schedule.
[20:04] Lina: One quick follow-up — when you do the pilot, will logs include raw prompts? We need them redacted.
[20:11] Jordan: We can redact or hash prompts; Dedicated can avoid storing request content entirely. We'll include the config options.
[20:20] [Short silence, some people typing]
[20:30] Alex: Alright thanks everyone. Quick logistics — I'll send calendar invite for pilot kickoff and include Priya's runbook. Any last questions?
[20:37] Marta: No, that's it. Thanks.
[20:40] Alex: Thanks all. Bye.

Notes on transcript quality: Automated transcription had some mis-attributed speaker labels early; product names in slides were abbreviated. There are occasional filler words, minor stutters, and imperfect punctuation.

References/shared artifacts: Edge cases deck: /redwood/edge-cases-deck.pdf, Console CSV export (will be attached), Optimize eval run link (to be shared).

End of transcript.
